Layouts of hexagons

Source: R/layout.R
layouts.Rd

These functions create a layout for the layout argument of hexmap(), which arranges the hexagons, and the hexagons of each group (e.g. state). Groups usually need a very different area of hexagons than they cover on the map (e.g. densely populated states have many small regions), so the map has to be distorted, and each layout distorts it differently. See vignette("layouts") for how they compare.

Usage

layout_diffusion(cartogram = 0.75, resolution = 256, proximity = 0.1)

layout_compact(anchor = NULL)

layout_slice(tree = NULL, anchor = NULL)

layout_hierarchy(shape = 0.4, resolution = 256, iterations = 30)

layout_repair(layout, iterations = 30, border = 0)

Arguments

cartogram

For layout_diffusion(), how far to warp the map, from 0 (keep the outline of the map, squeezing groups into it) to 1 (make each group's area proportional to its number of regions, distorting the outline). Each group's area is warped to area^(1 - cartogram) * size^cartogram, where size is its area in proportion to its number of regions.

resolution

For layout_hierarchy() and layout_diffusion(), the width of the grid used to find the diffusion cartogram, in cells (at least 16). Larger grids are more accurate for small groups but slower.

proximity

For layout_diffusion(), how much to keep each group's hexagons near its regions, from 0 upwards. Unless cartogram = 1, groups don't cover the area their regions need, so hexagons pass from group to group. Each hexagon is given to groups by its squared distance to the group's warped shape plus proximity times its squared distance to the group's nearest region, so that a group gives up the hexagons far from its regions (e.g. outback rather than near its cities). With 0, only the shapes are used.

anchor

For layout_compact() and layout_slice(), a data frame with columns group, x and y giving positions (in the coordinates of the map, after any transformation by the crs argument of hexmap()) to use in place of the centroids of some groups when arranging them. For example, moving a group's anchor east of its neighbour places its block on the east side of that neighbour.

tree

For layout_slice(), the order in which groups are cut apart, as a nested list of group names. Each list is cut into its elements, along whichever axis best separates them, and each character vector of several groups is cut automatically. For example, list("WA", list(list("NT", "SA"), list("QLD", "NSW", "VIC"))) first separates WA from the other states, then NT and SA from the eastern states. Every group must appear exactly once.

shape

For layout_hierarchy(), how far to restore each group's own shape after warping the map into a cartogram, from 0 (the cartogram) to 1 (a scaled copy of each group's shape). Larger values keep groups more recognisable, but values above about 0.5 can fold the map.

iterations

For layout_hierarchy() and layout_repair(), the number of swaps of hexagons between groups to try, per region, when adjusting the borders between groups (from 0 upwards). More iterations are slower, but more likely to make every group touch as on the map.

layout

For layout_repair(), the layout to repair, such as layout_compact().

border

For layout_repair(), how much to keep each region's distance to borders (the coast and each other group) when placing it, relative to keeping its position, from 0 upwards. Distances are measured from each region's polygon, in hexagon widths, and only up to 3 widths, so only regions near a border are held to it. With border = 1, a region one hexagon further from a border than on the map is as bad as a region one hexagon from its position. Larger values keep borders at the expense of the order of regions within groups. With 0, only regions of groups whose hexagons changed are placed again.

Value

A layout function, for the layout argument of hexmap().

Details

Without groups, all regions form a single group, which every layout keeps close to the outline of the map, except layout_compact(), which draws it as one compact block, and layout_slice(), which draws each landmass as a rectangle of hexagons. layout_diffusion() then places each region on the hexagon that minimises the total squared displacement of all regions, so no two regions swap their relative position.

  • layout_hierarchy() (the default) lays out the groups first, then the regions within each group. The groups are warped by a diffusion cartogram, blended towards a scaled copy of each group's own shape (by shape), so that groups keep their shapes while still touching their neighbours, at the expense of the outline of the whole map. The hexagons are split between groups nearest to these shapes, keeping groups with little coast (such as the ACT) off the edge of the hexagons, and the borders between groups are adjusted (by simulated annealing) so that groups touch as they do on the map. Regions are then placed within each group by matching the spread of the group on the map to the spread of its hexagons, so each group's regions keep their positions within it.

  • layout_diffusion() warps the map with a diffusion cartogram (Gastner & Newman, 2004), which grows or shrinks each group while keeping its shape and its borders with other groups. The hexagons tile the warped map, and are split between groups along the warped borders. cartogram sets how far the map is warped: with cartogram = 0 the outline of the map is kept and groups are squeezed into it, while with cartogram = 1 the area of each group is proportional to its number of regions and the outline is distorted to fit.

  • layout_compact() draws each group as a compact block of hexagons, in the style of hand drawn election maps. Each group is treated as a circle with the area of its hexagons, and the circles are arranged so that neighbouring groups keep their direction from each other (weighting longer shared borders more), then packed together without overlapping.

  • layout_slice() lays out groups as a spatial treemap (Wood & Dykes, 2008), so that the borders between groups are long straight lines. Each landmass is drawn as a rectangle of hexagons, which is recursively cut in two between rows or columns of hexagons, giving each side exactly the hexagons of its groups. Each cut is chosen so that neighbouring groups keep their relative position (e.g. one above the other for a horizontal cut) and pieces don't become thin.

layout_repair() wraps any layout to then adjust the borders between groups, so that groups touch where they share a border on the map, and don't touch where they don't. Pairs of hexagons are swapped across group borders (by simulated annealing), which keeps the hexagons of the layout, and keeps each group's hexagons contiguous and compact. Repairing a slice layout bends its straight borders. With border, the regions are then placed on their group's hexagons keeping their distances to borders as well as their positions: regions near the coast or another group stay near it, and regions away from borders stay away from them.

Arguments shared by layouts

An argument has the same name, meaning and default in every layout that takes it:

  • resolution (layout_hierarchy(), layout_diffusion()) is the size of the grid used to find the diffusion cartogram.

  • iterations (layout_hierarchy(), layout_repair()) is the number of hexagon swaps tried per region when adjusting the borders between groups.

  • anchor (layout_compact(), layout_slice()) moves where groups are placed relative to each other.

Arguments that set how far the map is distorted are named after what they change, and range from 0 to 1: cartogram is how far the whole map is warped towards a cartogram, and shape is how far each group is then restored to its own shape. Arguments that weigh one thing to keep against the position of regions are named after what they keep, range from 0 (ignore it) upwards, and keep it more as they increase: proximity (keep groups' hexagons near their regions) and border (keep regions' distances to borders).

Custom layouts

A layout is a function with arguments geometry (the regions' geometry), group (the group of each region, all equal without groups), land and cellsize (the width of the hexagons to use), which returns the hexagon of each region as an sfc of polygons. land is a list with the separately tiled landmasses as geometry, and the landmass of each region as region. Each group's hexagons should be contiguous on each landmass.

References

Gastner, M. T., & Newman, M. E. J. (2004). Diffusion-based method for producing density-equalizing maps. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 101(20), 7499–7504.

Wood, J., & Dykes, J. (2008). Spatially ordered treemaps. IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics, 14(6), 1348–1355.

Examples

library(sf)
# The 2025 Australian federal election, in Australian Albers
election <- st_transform(aus_election_2025, 3577)

# Compact blocks, with the ACT on the east side of NSW
nsw <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(st_union(election[election$state == "NSW", ])))
anchor <- data.frame(group = "ACT", x = nsw[1] + 5e5, y = nsw[2])
election_hex <- hexmap(election, group = state,
                       layout = layout_compact(anchor = anchor))

# \donttest{
# The other layouts take a few seconds each
# Each state keeps its shape, at the expense of the outline of Australia
election_hex <- hexmap(election, group = state,
                       layout = layout_hierarchy())
# Keep more of the outline of Australia
election_hex <- hexmap(election, group = state,
                       layout = layout_diffusion(cartogram = 0.5))
# Compact blocks that touch as the states do
election_hex <- hexmap(election, group = state,
                       layout = layout_repair(layout_compact()))
# }
